text: Inferring population connectivity in eastern massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) using landscape genetics. Assessing the environmental factors that influence the ability of a threatened species to move through a landscape can be used to identify conservation actions that connect isolated populations. However, direct observations of species’ movement are often limited, making the development of alternate approaches necessary. Here we use landscape genetic analyses to assess the impact of landscape features on the movement of individuals between local populations of a threatened snake, the eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus). We linked connectivity data with habitat information from two landscapes of similar size: a large region of unfragmented habitat and a previously studied fragmented landscape consisting of isolated patches of habitat. We used this analysis to identify features of the landscape where modification or acquisition would enhance population connectivity in the fragmented region. We found evidence that current connectivity was impacted by both contemporary land-cover features, especially roads, and inherent landscape features such as elevation. Next, we derived estimates of expected movement ability using a recently developed pedigree-based approach and least-cost paths through the unfragmented landscape. We then used our pedi- gree and resistance map to estimate resistance polygons of the potential extent for S. catenatus movement in the fragmented landscape. These polygons iden- tify possible sites for future corridors connecting currently isolated populations in this landscape by linking the impact of future habitat modification or land acquisition to dispersal ability in this species. Overall, our study shows how modeling landscape resistance across differently fragmented landscapes can identify habitat features that affect contemporary movement in threatened spe- cies in fragmented landscapes and how this information can be used to guide mitigation actions whose goal is to connect isolated populations.

Anthropogenic changes to landscapes can have significant impacts on the habitat of threatened species persisting in small, isolated populations, ranging from negative effects such as habitat fragmentation or habitat loss to positive impacts like promoting dispersal to unoccupied regions (Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2007; Johansson et al., 2007; Richardson, 2012). Negative impacts of habitat fragmentation and loss can lead to increased extinction risk due to changes in demographic factors, such as a reduced carrying capacity, as well as increasing the effects of genetic drift and inbreeding in newly isolated populations (Fahrig, 2017; Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2007; Pavlova et al., 2017). One approach to mitigating these negative impacts is through interventions such as the creation of corridors between currently isolated populations through targeted land management (Barrows et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2016). However, identification of potential landscape features and specific areas to modify can be problematic and should be based on research-driven management plans assessed for each species and location in a quantitative way Landscape genetics offers insight into both the genetic structure of populations and the environmental features driving observed patterns in genetic structure (Escoda et al., 2019; Klinga et al., 2019; Manel et al., 2003; Manel & Holderegger, 2013). Specifically, landscape genetics develops these insights by correlating spatial heterogeneity with estimates of genetic differentiation with goals ranging from estimating connectivity to understanding environmental factors driving adaptation (Manel & Holderegger, 2013). When used to assess connectivity, landscape genetic analyses can identify complete barriers to movement (i.e., large rivers, highways) and other features that hinder movement (i.e., dirt roads) (Baguette et al., 2013; Fletcher et al., 2016). A specific approach used for such analyses is the development of resistance models that can produce detailed estimates of landscape features that may hinder or promote connectivity (Mateo-Sanchez et al., 2015; Spear et al., 2010; By using resistance surfaces to quantify the impacts of landscape heterogeneity on movement, managers can predict optimal movement pathways or corridors to maximize conservation benefits (Epps et al., 2007; Segelbacher et al., 2010). Although numerous approaches have been used to create or identify resistance surfaces in landscape genetic analyses (Shirk et al., 2018; Spear et al., 2010), methods now exist that eliminate the subjectivity of expert opinion that was previously used to parameterize these models (Peterman, 2018). For example, one approach is to transform landscape features using a maximum-likelihood population-effects (MLPE) model to create pairwise resistance measures that best match observed genetic differences between individuals, which represents that landscape’s impact on connectivity (Peterman, 2018). Resistance maps can then be used to identify possible corridors or barriers to movement and identify regions where management activity may greatly improve the connectivity and hence viability of isolated populations (Crawford et al., 2016; Klinga et al., 2019; Ruiz-Lopez et al., 2016; Thatte et al., 2018). An important limitation of this resistance-based approach is that the results of landscape genetics studies are often specific to a particular study area and relevant only to the location analyzed (Zeller et al., 2012). This limitation can be overcome by conducting analyses across multiple independent study sites, but this can be difficult due to both sampling cost and the difficulty in finding similar sites to act as spatial replicates (Short Bull et al., 2011). Resistance maps also only provide relative values between all habitat patches used and cannot specifically be used to tell whether any two patches are directly connected via dispersal (Sawyer et al., 2011; Zeller et al., 2012). To circumvent these limitations, resistance maps can be related to the dispersal capabilities of a species to calculate the minimum number of resistance units between known dispersal events equivalent to known, realized dispersal abilities (Sawyer et al., 2011). The observed resistances can then be used to build movement polygons representing different probabilities of movement in any given landscape. The difficulty of identifying contemporary, known movement events can complicate the application of this approach. While mark-recapture studies and radiotelemetry are potential methods, both rely on observing relatively rare long-distance events (Nathan et al., 2003). One potential alternative is the use of pedigrees to find individuals with recent shared ancestors (Fountain et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2021a). Pairs of recently related individuals separated by geographic distances outside of expected home range sizes or habitat patches must have had at least one dispersal event occur to create the observed pattern (Fountain et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2021a). (2016) used such an approach incorporating first-order pedigree relationships between nesting females and offspring in Blanding’s turtles (Emydoidea blandingii) to infer local connectivity, whereas Escoda et al. (2019) and Fountain et al. (2018) used extended pedigrees from genetic data to model connectivity. However, all previous studies focused solely on the geographic distance between sample units and only qualitatively discussed the impacts of features of the intervening landscape patterns of movement. One reason for this may be the lack of quantitative approaches to assessing the influence of these features on movement.

Here we address this gap by developing approaches that link the results of landscape resistance models with estimates of contemporary movement based on individual pedigrees to calculate the minimum resistance values for movement events. This resistance minimum may be used as an estimate of the lower limit of dispersal as it sets a minimum threshold for known movements and can therefore be used for modeling realized dispersal, as proposed by Sawyer et al. This approach extends previous research by incorporating known dispersal events with landscape resistance models to generate quantitative estimates of realized dispersal for a given species. In this paper, we used this conceptual approach to evaluate the habitat features that impact connectivity between local populations of eastern massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) in Ohio. This species is a threatened rattlesnake that persists in small, isolated populations throughout the Midwestern United States and Canada (Hileman et al., 2017; Seigel, 1986; Gibbs & Chiucchi, 2012; Sovic et al., 2016, 2019). Understanding how individuals move through their environment is critical for determining extinction risks and promoting the colonization of habitat to increase population sizes (Faust et al., 2011; Hanski & Ovaskainen, 2003; Hileman et al., 2017; Shirk et al., 2010). Prior studies showed that these snakes rely on grasslands and wet meadows for movement and overwintering habitat (DiLeo et al., 2013; In regions with no barriers to movement, they can form a single admixed population over several kilometers (DiLeo et al., 2013; Kudla et al., 2021). In Ohio, most S. catenatus are found in one of two regions. One region is in Northeast (NE) Ohio and consists of many isolated sites with genetically distinct populations that show little or no contemporary connectivity (Martin et al., 2021a). In contrast, a second region, in Central Ohio, is likely to be a single genetic population due to its location within a single protected wildlife area, where habitat fragmentation is minimal (S. Martin, personal observation). For our analysis, we used these regions as independent replicates in analyses that had the following three goals: (1) Assess the effects of contemporary land cover and elevation on connectivity for two S. catenatus populations in Ohio found in fragmented (NE Ohio) and relatively unfragmented (Central Ohio) regions; (2) model the realized dispersal ability of S. catenatus in the fragmented NE Ohio population based on observed distances between known related individuals from the more contiguous population in Central Ohio; and (3) use the estimated dispersal capacity based on resistance and published movements to delineate potential dispersal polygons and predict how far an individual could move in an idealized landscape. We then propose that these estimated resistancebased polygons can be used to identify candidate regions for potential corridors that would facilitate movement between the isolated sites in NE Ohio. Broadly, our study develops a general approach that models landscape resistance across differently fragmented landscapes to identify habitat features that have direct impacts on contemporary movement in threatened species in fragmented habitats.

We used landscape genetic analyses of ddRAD genetic data sets of individuals from two regions to assess the impact of habitat characteristics on recent connectivity between S. catenatus populations. The first portion of the samples was previously sequenced as part of a published data set of 86 S. catenatus individuals from five sites located in highly fragmented habitat in NE Ohio (Martin et al., 2021a, Appendix S1: Figure S1). Each site consisted of one to four patches of habitat ranging in area from 0.3 to 2.5 ha, all within 20 m of each other. For the second set of samples, we generated ddRAD genetic data from newly collected samples from an additional 109 individuals sampled from six sites in contiguous habitat in Killdeer Plains Wildlife Area in Wyandot County, Ohio (Central Ohio; Figure 1). These six sites were used because they covered a geographic area (approximately 6 km2) similar to the previously studied region in NE Ohio. For each S. catenatus we collected a small blood and scale sample as well as Global Positioning System location information. Individuals had a passive integrated transponder (PIT tag) implanted to prevent double sampling by identifying recaptures of the same individual snake. For recaptures, we used the first sampling location in later analyses. To generate genetic data for these samples, we used the protocols outlined in Martin et al. In brief, we extracted DNA from blood and scale samples from S. catenatus samples collected in the Central Ohio region and then used EcoR1 and Pst1 restriction enzymes to fragment DNA followed by size selecting for fragments between 300 and 600 bp. DNA was then barcoded and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq platforms. After sequencing, raw reads were aligned using a draft assembly of a S. catenatus reference genome (Mathur et al., in preparation) and loci identified using ipyrad (version 0.9.53) (Eaton & Overcast, 2020), with a single bi-allelic single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) retained per locus to ensure all SNPs were unlinked. For an assessment of genetic structure in the NE Ohio region, we used the results of previous analyses of population genetic structure reported by Martin et al. To generate comparable results for samples from the unfragmented Central Ohio region, we analyzed the new data from this area using the same approach of Martin et al. Briefly, we imported the filtered genetic data into R (version 3.5.3) under RStudio (version 1.1.463) using the radiator package (Gosselin, 2020). Population structure was assessed following the two-step methodology of Martin et al. First, we calculated the number of probable clusters using the adegenet package by running the find.clusters algorithm followed by a discriminate analysis of principal components (DAPC) to select the optimal value of K without using sampling location as a prior in the model (Jombart et al., 2010). This method optimizes the number of groups based on minimizing the within-group genetic variance while maximizing the between-group variance and does not rely on any underlying assumptions of Hardy–Weinberg or linkage equilibrium (Jombart, 2008; Jombart & Ahmed, 2011; Jombart et al., 2010) and as such is not affected by closely related individuals. We then assessed the robustness of our individual assignments by comparing results to a DAPC analysis that included location-based priors. Next, we used the program conStruct as a spatially explicit alternative method to determine the potential number of genetic groups (Bradburd et al., 2018). ConStruct requires a user-supplied K value to optimize the assignment of individuals, and we used the three most likely values from the previous DAPC as priors to test. Once a K cluster value is given, conStruct groups individuals based on both the genetic and geographic distance between every pair. We then quantified the overall proportion of genetic variance that is explained by each group in the data set using the layer.contribution function. We selected the optimal K based on the recommended cut-off of the largest K where every group explains at least 10% of the overall genetic variance (Bradburd et al., 2018). Finally, to generate quantitative estimates of the degree to which clusters are genetically distinct, we also calculated Fst values between the six sampled sites using the adegenet package (Jombart et al., 2010).

We focused on land cover as our primary landscape feature due to the known importance of land-cover variation to S. catenatus movement and survival (DiLeo et al., 2013; McCluskey, 2016; McCluskey et al., 2018). Land cover is also greatly affected by anthropogenic impacts and so can be a target of management efforts (Keller et al., 2015; Additionally, we included elevation as a secondary component as this feature was likely to play a role in the historical formation of lowlands and wetlands important to S. catenatus habitat use and so may also impact the genetic structure of populations. Low-elevation areas may also be more likely to contain crayfish burrows important for overwintering for S. catenatus (Baker et al., 2020; Reinert & Kodrich, 1982). Although other factors such as canopy coverage and roads are known to greatly impact rattlesnake behavior (Clark et al., 2008), we did not include these variables because these features are already reflected in land-cover data as distinct forest classes, and impervious surface and overparameterization of resistance models using redundant variables should be avoided (Cushman & Landguth, 2010). We imported the 2016 US Geological Survey (USGS) National Land Cover Database (NLCD; Dewitz & USGS, 2019) and Digital Elevation Maps generated by the Ohio Geographically Referenced Information Program (OGRIP) as rasters using the raster package (Hijmans & van Etten, 2012). Using the NLCD land-cover types, Central Ohio can be characterized as largely grasslands (S. catenatus habitat) and cropland, with roads (impervious surface) throughout the landscape (Figure 1). In contrast, S. catenatus habitat in NE Ohio is separated by heavily forested areas, roads, and houses throughout the region (Figure 2). The Digital Elevation Maps were not relativized to each survey location but instead used absolute elevation. Elevation was similar in each region (NE Ohio minimum: 235 m, maximum: 292 m; Central Ohio minimum: 251 m, maximum: 298 m), justifying the use of absolute values. The NLCD is a 30-m resolution, Landsat-based, land-cover database across the United States maintained by the USGS and updated on a 5-year cycle. Due to the importance of herbaceous cover and “out-of-production” cropland for S. catenatus, we verified the accuracy of the NLCD raster by downloading five consecutive years of the USDA Cropland Data Layer representing annual agricultural production across the United States (USDA, 2019). We then converted the cropland categories into binary values, where 0 represented anything other than active crop production and 1 represented all active agriculture. We summed raster cell values over the 5 years, and if any cell had a score greater than 2, it was considered active cropland. We then used the new cropland raster to correct any cells in the NLCD raster to cropland that were likely miscategorized as a cover type other than cropland. rare or similar land-cover categories and reduce the number of parameters in the optimization model, we merged categories together as described in Appendix S1: Table S1. After applying corrections and merging our land-cover data, we were left with 10 discrete categories based on coarse landscape types in the final map (Appendix S1: Table S1). We also applied a correction to ensure continuous roads (impervious surface in the NLCD) by overlaying lines on roadways and converting all raster values under the line to impervious surface. Next, we used the ResistanceGA R package to optimize landscape resistance values based on the genetic distances and geographic locations of individuals across both regions simultaneously (Peterman, 2018). ResistanceGA optimizes landscape resistance values and can take multiple inputs for both categorical and continuous variables (Peterman, 2018). This allows for a wide range of potential values to be tested, and by using multiple runs with a stochastic optimization algorithm, the user can be confident in model optimization, meeting recommendations for statistical tests for landscape genetics (Keller et al., 2015). To process the genetic data for input into ResistanceGA, we calculated the genetic distance (proportion of shared alleles) between all pairs of individuals in each of our two regions. Specifically, we first calculated genetic distances between all pairs of individual S. catenatus in each region separately using the “propShared” function from the adegenet R package (Jombart et al., 2010). Next, we built a second matrix containing geographic distances between all individuals within each data set. We then created a single unified matrix containing the pairwise genetic distances for all individuals, with NA for comparisons between regions specifying that no comparisons were made between NE Ohio and Central Ohio individuals. We also made a matrix of “pairs to include” indicating which pairwise comparisons should be included when optimizing resistance values. We limited comparisons to those between individuals in the same region that were captured within 3 years of each other and were more than 250 m apart to focus on drivers of dispersal events between occupied survey sites. To minimize the potential effects of temporal variation between generations, we only compared individuals captured within 3 years (approximately one generation) of each other. Once the genetic distance matrix, geographic distance matrix, and exclusion matrix were created, we ran ResistanceGA to fit resistance values on both land cover and elevation as a unified model. Model fit was assessed by the pseudo-R2 value and the relative contribution (proportion of variation explained) of each landscape was calculated to assess the relative importance of historical factors (elevation) compared to contemporary anthropogenic impacts (land cover). We then compared the relative resistance values for each land-cover class to determine which features were most important to the genetic structuring of S. catenatus. The final raster containing optimized resistance values across both landscapes was generated for use in calculating dispersal.

After calculating optimized resistance values, we estimated the likely maximum effective distance an individual S. catenatus had dispersed based on our resistance map. We measured resistance between pairs of recently related (within three generations, or 5–30 years based on the life span of S. catenatus) individuals representing realized dispersal over a timescale that matches the landcover data set. To do this, we first identified any pairs of closely related individuals that would represent known recent dispersal events (Martin et al., 2021a, 2021b) in a situation where movement is minimally impacted by habitat fragmentation. For this reason, we focused our analysis of dispersal on the more contiguous habitat in Central Ohio rather than the fragmented landscape of the NE Ohio region (Martin et al., 2021a). Additionally, no probable dispersal events had been observed in past studies of NE Ohio, matching the genetic structuring observed there (Martin et al., 2021a). To detect dispersal events, we first generated a pedigree using the R package sequoia following the same protocol given in Martin et al. (2021a, 2021b) to find any pairs of related individuals in the Central Ohio region. We required all potential pedigree pairs to be 95% more likely than any other possible relationship to be retained in the final pedigree (Martin et al., 2021a). We chose this high threshold due to the high rates of inbreeding seen in other populations of S. catenatus (Martin et al., 2021a). We then used the optimized resistance map described earlier to calculate least-cost paths (LCPs) using the R package leastcostpaths between all kin pairs in Central Ohio (Lewis, 2021). These LCPs represent the minimum resistance (“realized dispersal”) that individuals would have had to move to produce the observed patterns. Finally, we used the maximum observed dispersal event as an estimate of the minimum potential for dispersal capability of these snakes over landscapes minimally impacted by habitat fragmentation. We compared our estimate of the dispersal capacity estimated from Central Ohio through measures of home range sizes and longdistance dispersal events inferred from radio telemetry and mark-recapture data inferred for this species rangewide and for the most geographically similar study that we could identify in the literature that was located in southern Michigan (Bailey et al., 2012).

After calculating an observed maximum resistance value for S. catenatus movement, we generated realized dispersal polygons (resistance polygon) representing how far individuals would travel using the LCP maximum estimate in both regions. These resistance polygons allowed us to determine whether sites in NE Ohio and Central Ohio could potentially have individuals moving between them and to identify specific locations where corridors could be generated to link currently isolated habitat patches (Kaszta et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2021a). We first delineated occupied sites by drawing polygons dividing the edge of open herbaceous grasslands to roads and forests—woody encroachment is a major threat to S. catenatus in Ohio, which assisted in the proper identification of habitat edges (Faust et al., 2011). To generate polygons, we used the “Distance Accumulation” function in ArcMap (ArcGIS version 10.1), using the centroid of each known occupied site in each region as a starting point, similar to the cumulative resistance kernel models implemented in Kaszta et al. Finally, we compared the resistance-informed estimates of potential dispersal with straight distance-based estimates of potential dispersal using published estimates of movement for S. catenatus. This also allowed us to identify specific locations for possible habitat links between isolated populations in NE Ohio. We then buffered occupied sites using published movement data for S. catenatus that reflect qualitative estimates of expected movement in unfragmented habitats. The first buffer covered 1 km around each site, representing the maximum home range size reported by DiLeo et al. (2013) for S. catenatus in an unfragmented landscape. The second buffer was extended to 2 km, based on the maximum long-distance movement documented via radio telemetry by Weatherhead and Prior (1992). Both values represent approximate estimates of the largest reported values for this species. Each buffer thus represented the absolute maximum an individual S. catenatus might travel outside of known sites as part of home range (1 km) or dispersal (2 km) movements if such movements are only constrained by geographic distance. Buffer shapefiles were generated in ArcMap using the “buffer” tool around each occupied site, without dissolving overlapping areas to visualize if sites could potentially be connected.

After sequencing samples, we removed all individuals with less than one million raw reads, leaving a total of 103 S. catenatus sampled across five survey sites in the Central Ohio region, as compared to the 86 individuals from the NE Ohio region (Figure 1, Martin et al., 2021a). This yielded a final data set for Central Ohio that consisted of a total of 1481 unlinked bi-allelic loci across 99 individuals, with four individuals excluded due to a high amount of missing data.

Our DAPC analysis in adegenet supported a single genetic cluster across all survey sites in Central Ohio. This contrasts with the five genetically distinct S. catenatus populations in NE Ohio reported by Martin et al. (2021a, 2021b) over a roughly equivalent 6-km2 area. When using the capture site as a prior, we found a high degree of uncertainty in assignment for individuals likely due to past admixture between sites. Consistent with these results, we also found low Fst values (mean = 0.027) across all pairs of sites (Appendix S1: Table S4A,B). Based on the results from the DAPC, we tested for the presence of K = 1, 2, and 3 clusters at the Central Ohio site using the spatially explicit model in conStruct using 10 independent runs of each K. We then selected the top run for each K value based on visual convergence of the Markov chain Monte Carlo method (10,000 iterations, 1000 burn-in period; Bradburd et al., 2018). ConStruct supported two genetic groups, since a third group only explained an additional 2% of the total genetic variation, well under the 10% threshold recommended for adding additional groups (Figure 1, Table 1, Bradburd et al., 2018). Compared to DAPC, conStruct found a weak east–west divide, centered around a north–south roadway. However, conStruct also found individuals showing shared ancestry in both areas of the Central Ohio site, matching expectations for a single genetic unit (Figure 1).

Estimate of best model for landscape resistance values We evaluated what features might account for variation in connectivity between S. catenatus in different locations T A B L E 1 Amount of genetic variation based on allelic covariance between individuals in each group of Sistrurus catenatus in Central Ohio region under conStruct models for K = 1, 2, 3.

by assessing the top landscape resistance model fit to elevation and land cover (Figure 2). After merging landcover and elevation data from Central and NE Ohio we found a single best model with a marginal pseudo-R2 value of 0.48. Overall, variation in land cover explained 54% of the average resistance per raster cell, whereas elevation explained the remaining 46%. Impervious surface was the single highest driver of resistance, matching expectations based on prior literature (Table 2; Clark et al., 2008). Herbaceous fields and pastures did not have the lowest resistance, despite this being the major habitat for S. catenatus in these regions, likely due to the fact that we excluded geographically close pairs of individuals. Specifically, our choice to exclude within-site pairs in our resistance model probably inflated the values for herbaceous cover because we did not include pairs of genetically similar individuals separated only by short stretches of habitat. Elevation contributed substantially to resistance in NE Ohio, where a river situated in the center of the site increased resistance between all S. catenatus populations. In contrast, elevation was of limited importance in the flatter Central Ohio site (Figure 2). In the more variable NE Ohio location, elevation showed a “Goldilocks zone” where both high and low extremes increased resistance based on a nonlinear transformation implemented in ResistanceGA. Other than elevation, roads (and impervious surfaces generally) act as a major barrier for S. catenatus movement in both regions. Roads were previously shown to rapidly fragment rattlesnake species due to high mortality rates in crossing (Clark et al., 2008). Cropland was another major driver of high resistance in the model that was second only to impervious surfaces. Overall, our best model found that both anthropogenic landscape features and elevation (or intrinsic landscape features correlated to elevation such as water table depth, surface moisture, or humidity) contributed to the lack of connectivity in NE Ohio S. catenatus populations. In preliminary models of individual regions, NE Ohio showed patterns and model fit that were similar to those of the merged model, while overall fit for Central Ohio was poor without including both regions (Appendix S1: Tables S2 and S3).

In Central Ohio, we found 35 pairs of closely related (within the past three generations) individuals, eight of which occurred between different survey sites. This was lower than the 110 closely related pairs reported in Martin et al. (2021a, 2021b) for NE Ohio, likely because the population size is much greater in the Central Ohio location (G. Lipps, personal communication, 2020), making it less likely to randomly sample closely related individuals. We also retained several pairs whose pedigree included unsampled intermediate individuals (e.g., grandparent–grandchild samples) for calculating possible dispersal distances. Using such pairs for movement estimates assumes a single dispersal event instead of the alternative of two dispersal events by closely related kin across generations. Given the rarity of longdistance dispersal events in these snakes (e.g., Marin et al., 2021), we feel this is a reasonable assumption. Figure 2c shows the distribution of LCPs for related individuals based on resistance units using the optimized map generated as described in the previous section. Although data are sparse, the distribution has the shape typical of a heavily right-skewed distribution commonly observed for dispersal distances for many vertebrates in which rare data points in the right tail of the distribution reflect infrequent but biologically important and informative long-distance dispersal events (Lowe, 2010; Trakhtenbrot et al., 2005). Although this related pair represented a grandchild–grandparent, this LCP corresponds to a geographic straight-line distance of approximately 1.1-km straight-line distance between sampled individuals located between distinct sampling locations and likely represents one dispersal event. Since an individual moving this straight-line distance at this site would have likely traversed nonhabitat (roads and cropland), we consider this to represent an observation of a rare long-distance dispersal event rather than movement within a single home range. Given this interpretation, we used a parameter value of 3000 resistance units to generate our resistance polygons (“realized dispersal”) that reflects potential movement taking landscape resistance into account for populations in both NE and Central Ohio locations (Figure 3). We then compared these resistance polygons with the 1-km buffers (“maximum home range”) and 2-km buffers (“geographic dispersal”), which represent potential movement unconstrained by fragmentation. We did not include the 0.1-km home ranges reported for similar Michigan populations of S. catenatus (Bailey et al., 2012) because they would be entirely within the current habitat patches, further justifying our assumption that the 1.1-km movement was a dispersal event. For NE Ohio, after constructing each movement buffer, no resistance polygons linked any pairs of adjacent populations (Figure 3a). However, both the home range and geographic dispersal buffers overlapped for multiple sites (Figure 3a). Our results support the hypothesis that S. catenatus is currently unlikely to disperse between existing sites in NE Ohio. In contrast, in Central Ohio (Figure 3b), almost all sites were connected even at the 25% resistance distance (750 resistance units), matching results from conStruct suggesting a single genetic unit.

supported our hypothesis that snakes in this region form a single genetic population. Specifically, DAPC supported K = 1, while conStruct found evidence for two genetic groups with frequent admixture observed between the potential groups (Figure 1). These results match prior studies of S. catenatus that show minimal genetic structure in populations found in contiguous habitats (DiLeo et al., 2013). This single large genetic unit contrasts with the previously studied NE Ohio populations that occupy a similarly sized area but are fragmented into five distinct genetic units (Martin et al., 2021a). Comparison of these studies strongly supports a role for habitat fragmentation that has a substantial impact on dispersal and genetic structure in S. catenatus. These findings match prior studies showing that snakes, like most reptiles, are sensitive to fragmentation (Breininger et al., 2011; Clark et al., 2010; Major et al., 2020; Rautsaw et al., 2018).

Our resistance model found impervious surface area (mainly due to roads and houses in this region) to be the single most likely barrier to movement. The impacts of roads are well documented in snakes (Clark et al., 2010; Shepard, 2008; Wagner et al., 2021; Weatherhead & Prior, 1992). This is also supported by the conStruct results of two potential weakly differentiated genetic groups in Central Ohio defined by a road that bisects the reserve. Of interest, herbaceous land cover was not the lowest resistance class, despite this being the primary habitat for S. catenatus in both study sites. This is likely an artifact due to the choice to exclude comparisons between individuals occurring within a single sampling site. Although scrub/shrub was the second highest resistance land cover, this is a rare feature in the landscape and can also be disregarded when identifying major features affecting connectivity (Table 2). Given these issues, we conclude that impervious surface and cropland are the two major land-cover classes with the largest impact on snake movement and are thus relevant to management actions that modify these features to increase connectivity between isolated populations (Table 2). The role of elevation in shaping genetic resistance is surprising, but it is likely because this feature captures important microhabitat features not included in land cover per se. As mentioned earlier, S. catenatus must overwinter underground and often rely on crayfish burrows to get far enough below the surface so as not to freeze (Johnson, 2000). Thus, elevation may represent proximity for the water table. At higher elevations, crayfish and the burrows they create are likely rarer due to increased depth of the water table, which decreases the availability of overwintering spots, whereas at low elevation S. catenatus may not be able to get below the frost line before soil becomes flooded, increasing drowning risk. Owing to variation in elevation driving microhabitat availability, S. catenatus in NE Ohio may have had moderate to low historical connectivity (Chiucchi & Gibbs, 2010) that was curtailed as human impacts increased effective distances beyond the movement abilities of most individuals. Other studies also found higher levels of genetic heterozygosity than expected given the current small genetic and census population sizes in NE Ohio, adding further evidence that the populations’ isolation is a recent phenomenon (Martin et al., 2021a; Sovic et al., 2019). There are several important caveats with respect to our estimates of landscape resistance. First, we only tested two landscape features in our model due to the limitations on the availability of fine-grained geographic information system (GIS) data, our focus on features that could be targeted by management plans, and our aim to minimize the risk of overparameterizing our model. This runs the risk of failing to include an important but unidentified habitat variable. However, these limitations are inherent in most landscape studies due to both the cost and difficulty of developing fine-grained data layers and standardizing variables across multiple sites. Second, our resistance maps were parameterized using land-cover and elevation data estimated over coarse spatial scales; the choice of scale can affect analyses and resistance surfaces and should be considered depending on data availability (Bauder et al., 2021; Winiarski et al., 2020). Third, our analyses are focused on landscapes occupied by S. catenatus in Ohio, and so the degree to which the results can be generalized to other populations is unknown. Finally, although ResistanceGA optimized values for each cover type, the methodology described here still relied on expert opinion in the generation of our merged cover types. However, we note that, although our final resistance values are specific to this study, the overall pattern (high fragmentation driven by roads and other human development) agrees with prior research both on this species (DiLeo et al., 2013) and on snakes and reptiles in general (Clark et al., 2010; Colino-Rabanal & Lizana, 2012).

Developing methods for linking habitat resistance maps to dispersal potential of individuals has been a significant research goal in landscape genetics (Kaszta et al., 2020; Macdonald et al., 2018; Sawyer et al., 2011). Here we used the novel approach of analyzing genetic pedigrees to identify recent dispersal events by individuals. We then used landscape genetics to model the resistance of a region to movement based on multiple features. We synthesized these results together by estimating the number of resistance units between pedigree pairs and applied these results to make inferences about potential versus realized dispersal in landscapes. Our methods are broadly applicable across taxa and landscapes and can be used as a general approach to explicitly link resistance maps with estimates of dispersal capacity. We acknowledge that our analysis relies heavily on our estimate of maximum realized dispersal in our “control” (minimally fragmented) landscape and that in this study this is based on a single long-distance dispersal event in the Central Ohio population (Figure 2c). Clearly, additional examples of long-distance movements would provide a stronger inference for our estimate of realized dispersal, but we feel our estimate is reasonable for number of reasons. First, as pointed out earlier, given the expected right skew and long tail of distributions of dispersal distances, long-distance events are expected to be rare and difficult to detect (Lowe, 2010; Trakhtenbrot et al., 2005). The fact that the shape of the observed distances in the Central Ohio region has the expected shape of such a distribution suggests that this single observation is not an outlier but is a typical data point that is a reasonable first approximation of values from the long tail of such a distribution. Second, the linear distance of this observed resistance value (1.1 km) is much greater than expected values of 0.1-km2 home range estimates from a geographically close population in Michigan (Bailey et al., 2012), supporting the argument that this observation represents a long-distance dispersal event. Nonetheless, we recognize the limitations of our inferences based on these data and emphasize that they should be considered a minimum estimate of realized dispersal ability since long-distance movements are difficult to document, and so other rare longer movements over longer distances may go undetected (Trakhtenbrot et al., 2005). In any study, documenting the upper value of long-distance movement will likely be challenging since this method relies on finding pairs of related individuals, which may be rare in large populations (Martin et al., 2021a). Our results provide a mechanistic explanation for the high degree of isolation shown by S. catenatus populations in the fragmented NE Ohio region that in some cases are separated by a distance of only 1.2 km. Under our buffers of dispersal focused on geographic distance, we would have expected sites in NE Ohio to show regular connectivity, but no pairs of populations in NE Ohio were connected based on the resistance polygons.

Based on the clear structure seen in the genetic data, movement between populations in the present landscape is extremely rare, matching out resistance polygons and not predictions based on the 2-km dispersal buffer (Figure 3). However, one pair of individuals from Central Ohio represented a dispersal event of 1.1 km, which is only slightly greater than the 1-km home range buffer (snakes in GRLL-3 and GRLL-4 populations respectively—see Martin et al., 2021a). If snakes dispersed >2 km (within known dispersal capabilities for this species; Weatherhead & Prior, 1992), this would lead to all sites forming a single metapopulation, which might have been the historical state for this region before human impacts led to fragmented habitats (Samarasin et al., 2017). This would be consistent with the observation by Martin et al. (2021a, 2021b) that, despite essentially complete isolation over contemporary timescales, some pairwise Fst values are still relatively low, suggesting that there likely had once existed a connectivity between the closest pairs of populations (Appendix S1: Table S4). In earlier studies, a single individual was captured in GRLL-4 while being genetically assigned to GRLL-3, showing that rare dispersal events between genetic units may still be possible in NE Ohio despite the current high resistance landscape (Martin et al., 2021a). These considerations reinforce our interpretation that a value of 3000 resistance units is likely an underestimate of the actual maximum dispersal capability for this species in this region, although the extent to which this is the case is unclear. Finally, a practical value of our results is that it provides managers with specific targets for locations for habitat management actions that will improve connectivity between currently isolated populations in NE Ohio. For example, habitat activity to increase connectivity between the GRLL-3 and GRLL-4 sites (Martin et al., 2021a) would be a reasonable management goal as both populations fall within the same 2-km polygon (Figure 3). Our resistance map and resistance polygons (Figure 3) can be used to identify high resistance locations that could be modified to decrease resistance to dispersal by, for example, converting active cropland to pastures or similar herbaceous grassland. Our maps can indicate specific sections of roadways that currently block dispersal and therefore may be candidates for the installation of underpasses and exclusion fences to minimize road mortality by directing animals to passages (Glista et al., 2009).

Other researcher have shown the potential for resistance surfaces to be used for modeling connectivity, but they have often relied on professional opinion to convert dispersal distances to resistance units (Kaszta et al., 2020). Our methodology can be widely used in landscape genetics to provide researchers with estimates of dispersal capabilities specific to their resistance surfaces. Our study also provides a specific example of how one commonly used landscape genetics analysis program, ResistanceGA (Peterman, 2018), can be used to optimize over multiple separate landscapes to reduce the biases associated with single landscape models when generating site-independent estimates of dispersal capacity (Zeller et al., 2012). The framework we present is easily generalizable and will allow studies on landscape genetics to both more clearly link resistance units to realized movements for a species and incorporate study sites separated by any distance.
